Text: Compared with DNA synthesis, RNA synthesis {{c1::does not::does or does not}} require a preexisting primer strand. RNA chains are initiated {{c1::de novo::Latin phrase}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: RNA synthesis differs from DNA synthesis in three ways: (1) the precursors are ribonucleoside triphosphates rather than deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates, (2) only one DNA strand is used as template in any given region, and (3) no primer is needed.

Pitfall: chain growth itself is the same as in DNA synthesis: 5′→3′, each ribonucleotide added to the 3′-hydroxyl group at the end of the chain with elimination of pyrophosphate.
verified_against: p279: 'RNA chains can be initiated de novo, without any requirement for a preexisting primer strand.' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p279: 'RNA synthesis occurs by a mechanism that is similar to that of DNA synthesis (Chapter 10) except that (1) the precursors are ribonucleoside triphosphates rather than deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates, (2) only one strand of DNA is used as a template for the synthesis of a complementary RNA chain in any given region, and (3) RNA chains can be initiated de novo, without any requirement for a preexisting primer strand.' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p279: 'The synthesis of RNA chains, like DNA chains, occurs in the 5′ 3′ direction, with the addition of ribonucleotides to the 3′-hydroxyl group at the end of the chain' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p279: 'The reaction involves a nucleophilic attack by the 3′-OH on the nucleotidyl (interior) phosphorus atom of the ribonucleoside triphosphate precursor with the elimination of pyrophosphate, just as in DNA synthesis.'

Text: An RNA transcript is {{c1::complementary::sequence relationship}} and {{c1::antiparallel::parallel or antiparallel}} to the DNA {{c2::template::template or nontemplate}} strand, but {{c1::identical (with U in place of T)::sequence relationship}} to the DNA {{c2::nontemplate::template or nontemplate}} strand.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: the template strand is the DNA strand that is actually transcribed (read by RNA polymerase); the nontemplate strand is the one not transcribed, which is why the RNA ends up matching it.

Pitfall: 'identical to the nontemplate strand' includes polarity: written 5′→3′, the RNA has the same polarity as the nontemplate strand and is antiparallel only to the template strand.

Distinguish: an mRNA is a coding (sense) strand of RNA because its sequence specifies amino acids; an RNA complementary to an mRNA is antisense RNA.

Text:
Transcription has three stages, in order:

(1) {{c1::initiation}}

→ (2) {{c1::elongation}}

→ (3) {{c1::termination}} of transcription and release of the nascent RNA molecule
Back Extra:
Mechanism: in initiation the polymerase binds a promoter and starts the chain at a nearby start site; in elongation it adds ribonucleotides 5′→3′ inside a locally unwound transcription bubble; in termination synthesis stops and the nascent (newly made) RNA is let go.

Distinguish: only initiation needs the sigma (σ) factor; once the chain has started, σ is released and elongation is carried out by the core enzyme (α2ββ′).

Text:
Each kind of subunit in the E. coli RNA polymerase holoenzyme has its own job:

α → {{c1::helps assemble the tetrameric core (α2ββ′)}}

β → {{c1::contains the ribonucleoside triphosphate (rNTP) binding site}}

β′ → {{c1::harbors the DNA template-binding region}}

σ → {{c1::recognizes promoters and binds the polymerase to them}}
Back Extra:
Why: σ works only at the start: sigma plays no role in chain elongation and is released once the RNA chain has been initiated, leaving the core enzyme (α2ββ′) to elongate.

Cue: promoters are also called transcription-initiation sites, so σ's whole job is to find where transcription should start.

Mnemonic: the Prime subunit (β′) holds the Pattern (the DNA template); plain β holds the Building blocks (the rNTPs).
